source_title: Interview | Author Elif Shafak on how she found a kindred spirit in Gustave Flaubert

Turkish-British writer Elif Shafak was shortlisted for the Booker Prize in 2019.
At a time when our existence seems reduced to a data point, the words of Turkish-British writer Elif Shafak feel diaphanous, allowing thoughts and emotions to expand into something more. Sometimes, they take the form of a colour, an image or a taste that refuses to disappear. They leave an imprint on the page, making space for human endeavour. Yet, lately, words have also become seeds of divisiveness, usurped by AI and deployed as instruments of distraction.
When Shafak found herself in despair, she turned to literature in search of a kindred spirit and found one in Gustave Flaubert. Born more than two centuries ago, the French novelist is regarded as a pioneer of realism who gave voice to society’s pariahs. In her latest book, In One Brief Moment All Eternity (Penguin), Shafak brings Flaubert’s inner world to life through a first-person narrative, portraying a man deeply attuned to the suffering of the dispossessed. Alongside it unfolds a third-person narrative in which 30 women, including his mother, his nursemaid, a circus star, an Egyptian dancer, the corpse of a prostitute he once saw and, of course, his most iconic heroine, Emma, reclaim the space to tell their stories.
